pairs.difference: A: the umbrella is tipped on a diagonal, and the canopy is seen from slightly below and to the side, with its panels foreshortened unevenly. This is a lively 3/4 view like the real cards. B: the saucer floats dead centre, seen from a fairly high and evenly level camera. The whole top deck is one flat green normal patch and the rim lights are spaced symmetrically. It is the frontal, whole-object-in-the-middle view that the lessons mark as generated.
pairs.fix: Bring the camera closer and lower, turn the saucer about 30 degrees so one side of the rim comes toward the viewer and looks bigger, tilt it slightly off level, and let the near rim edge come close to the card border.

pairs.difference: A: the rocket is drawn as an almost flat side-on cutout on a diagonal. The fins read as flat cards with no turn into depth, the body shows no foreshortening, and the cloud layers are shapes behind it with no depth gap. B: the plane is in a strong 3/4 view, with the near wing and engine larger, the far wing receding, and the tail cut off by the frame. That matches the real cards' closer, turned camera.
pairs.fix: Turn the rocket so it flies toward the viewer at 3/4: show the nose bigger and nearer, put one fin in front overlapping the body and the far fin smaller behind it, and let the flame or a fin cross the card edge.

pairs.difference: A: the balloons overlap in depth, with the front teal balloon covering the red and purple ones, and the strings converge to a knot. That gives clear foreground and back layers. B: the yellow saucer is seen almost exactly side-on at eye level and centred, with both thrusters showing symmetrically. There is barely any top surface and no turn, so it reads as a flat profile.
pairs.fix: Raise the camera slightly and turn the saucer about 30 degrees so its top dome and one end come toward the viewer, with the near thruster larger than the far one. Move in closer so the hull fills more of the card.

pairs.difference: Both cards look steeply down on a wooden table. A: the folded map has fold ridges that catch different normals, and the magnifier stands up out of it, making a clear foreground layer over the map, with the map running off the card edge. B: the star chart is a single flat board with near-parallel edges and almost no convergence. Its normal map is one even patch (0.92 planar), and nothing rises off it, so there is no depth layer between the board and the table.
pairs.fix: Lower the camera to a 3/4 angle so the board's far edge clearly shrinks, show its thick side edge, prop one corner up or lay an object such as a compass on it so something overlaps the board, and let one corner run past the card edge.

pairs.difference: A: the ice tray is seen in 3/4 from a medium-high camera, with the table edge running diagonally under it. B: the paddling pool is seen from a high angle, with the fence corner converging behind it and grass as a consistent ground plane. Both hold one view and a consistent ground, so the viewpoint gives no reason to choose.

A: the energy cell is dead centre and perfectly symmetric, seen from straight in front, with matching top and bottom caps. Its ground is only a soft gradient and its shadow barely anchors it. B: the vending machine is turned 3/4, with the side panel visible, and its feet sit on a ground line. That is the real cards' turned camera.
pairs.fix: Turn the canister about 30 degrees and raise the camera a little so you see down onto its top cap, with the ellipses of the top and bottom caps clearly different. Set its base on a visible surface with a contact shadow, and move in closer so it fills the card.

pairs.difference: A: the sandcastle is seen nearly front-on, with the bucket and spade in the foreground, the sea and sky behind, and a consistent sand ground. B: the bumper car is seen at 3/4 from a low, close camera, the pole runs off the top of the card, and the floor recedes. Both read as real-card viewpoints.

A: the drone floats dead centre with lots of empty space around it, seen from a high, evenly level camera. All four rotors are flat green normal discs of almost the same size, so there is little difference between near and far. B: the lamp is close and cropped at the bottom, the head is seen from slightly below, and the curved arm overlaps the post. That matches the real cards' tight framing.
pairs.fix: Bring the camera much closer and lower, tilt the drone so the front two rotors are noticeably bigger than the back two and one rotor overlaps the card edge, and fill most of the card with the drone.

pairs.difference: A: the lighthouse (a real card in the lessons) is close, cropped at the bottom, and seen from a low camera. B: the antenna mast is a small figure standing far back on a wide, empty rooftop. The floor plane takes up most of the card at a steep angle, and the hero is tiny, with a long shadow. The camera is too far away and the ground dominates.
pairs.fix: Move the camera in close and low so the mast fills the card from bottom to top, crop the base at the bottom edge, and keep only a sliver of sky and roof behind it.

pairs.difference: A: the rover sits whole in the middle of a wide lunar ground plane, seen from a high 3/4 camera. All four wheels and the full chassis are visible, and there is a lot of empty ground around it. B: the bicycle is close and cropped by the card edges, the car behind overlaps it, and the road recedes. That gives tight, layered depth like the real cards.
pairs.fix: Move the camera closer and lower, let the near front wheel get large and cross the card edge, crop the antenna dish at the top, and shrink the visible empty ground.

pairs.difference: A: the guidebook is seen from a high 3/4 view, with its thick page block and spine clearly turned toward the viewer and the bookmarks sticking out in depth. B: the tablet is a thin slab seen almost straight down. Its normal map is one even sheet (0.95 planar, above the real range), the side edge is barely visible, and nothing sits in front of it.
pairs.fix: Lower the camera to a 3/4 angle so the tablet's far edge clearly shrinks and its thick rounded side edge shows, prop it up on a small stand or tilt it toward the viewer, and let one corner run off the card.

pairs.difference: A: the sneakers are a pair overlapping in depth at a 3/4 angle, with the near shoe larger, on a clear floor line. B: the helmet sits centred and almost straight-on at eye level, with the visor facing the viewer and the collar rings drawn as level, symmetric bands. There is little turn and no overlap layer.
pairs.fix: Turn the helmet about 35 degrees so the visor faces off to one side and the side ear-piece is nearer and larger, raise the camera slightly to see over the top of the shell, and frame it tight.

pattern: Generated cards put the whole object dead centre with empty space around it, seen from an evenly level or straight-on camera. Near and far parts end up nearly the same size. Flat items (boards, tablets) are shown from almost straight above as single even normal patches. Large empty ground planes shrink the hero. Real cards frame the object tighter, turn it into a clear 3/4 view, let it overlap or cross the card edge, and build depth by stacking parts in front of each other.
